name: Church of São Francisco
short: A Gothic church of 1383–1410 with one of Portugal's most opulent Baroque gilded interiors and catacombs beneath the altar.
long: The Church of São Francisco is Porto's finest Gothic building: a three-nave church with a transept, built between 1383 and 1410. It is best known, however, for its interior, which in the first half of the 18th century was clad in Baroque gilded woodcarving across walls, columns, chapels and vaults. The sheer quantity of gold, the Tree of Jesse altarpiece and the catacombs below make it one of the city's most remarkable churches. It also preserves a rare medieval mural, the Madonna of the Rose.
history:
The Franciscans settled in Porto in the early 13th century and were granted land for a church in 1233. Disputes with the bishop over the boundaries of their precinct and resistance from the established clergy delayed the work for years; Pope Innocent V intervened with the bull Doelentis accepimus of 1244, confirming the order's hold on the land. The foundations of the monastery and a first, more modest single-nave church were then laid.

In 1383, by decree of King Ferdinand, a special protector of the Franciscans, work began on the present church, completed in 1410. The new building was considerably larger: three naves of five bays, a projecting transept and a three-part chevet ringed by buttresses. It is the finest example of Gothic architecture in Porto; under King John I a rare mural, the Madonna of the Rose, attributed to António Florentim, was painted here.

In the 15th and 16th centuries prominent Porto families became patrons of the monastery, funding the side chapels. One of the most notable is the chapel of Saint John the Baptist, built in the 1530s for the Carneiro family to a design by João de Castilho in the Manueline style.

The main artistic campaign took place in the first half of the 18th century, when almost every interior surface — walls, columns, side chapels and ceiling — was covered in Baroque gilded woodcarving. Altarpieces were made by Filipe da Silva, António Gomes, Manuel da Costa Andrade and others; the Tree of Jesse (1718–1721) is considered the most lavish treatment of that theme in Portugal.

In 1833 a fire, started by gunfire from Miguelite troops during the siege of Porto, destroyed the monastic buildings. The ruined cloister was demolished to make way for the Stock Exchange Palace. After the male religious orders were suppressed in 1834, the church served as a customs warehouse until 1839. It was declared a national monument in 1910. Beneath it lie catacombs holding the remains of friars, now open as part of the museum.
facts: The Franciscans were granted the land in 1233; a papal bull confirmed it in 1244.
The present church was built in 1383–1410 under King Ferdinand.
Its interior was clad in Baroque gilded woodcarving in the first half of the 18th century.
The Tree of Jesse altarpiece was made in 1718–1721.
The monastery burnt in 1833; the church was a customs warehouse from 1834 to 1839.
The Madonna of the Rose mural dates from the reign of King John I.
A national monument since 1910, with catacombs beneath the church.
tip: Entry is paid and includes the catacombs and museum; come in the morning before the tour groups build up. The church is steps from the Stock Exchange Palace, so visit the two together. Inside it is dark and very gold — avoid flash and let your eyes adjust. The nearest metro is São Bento, then walk towards Ribeira.
